Historians today find themselves in a better position than their counterparts in the
past: the explosion of knowledge and flood of disclosure that characterize our age provide
researchers with access to a plethora of sources--materials that in previous eras were jealously
guarded in archives, watched over by institutions and authorities that impeded historians wishing to
unlock their mysteries. Yet it is doubtful whether the influence exerted by historians today on the
shaping of collective public memory has actually grown as a result of greater access.

This article focuses on the complex relationship between historical scholarship and collective
memory as exemplified in a concrete instance. Such scholarship endeavors to be based on
impartial and objective research and authentic documentary sources, striving to present a picture of
reality (either factual or mental) as close as possible to the picture emerging from the
documentation. Collective memory, by contrast, is the picture of reality present in the public
imagination at a given moment, an image-complex reflective of the spirit of the times and the
emphases of the era, its ideologies and social needs. A central contention here is that, despite the
expansion of the areas of historical research, the burgeoning numbers of investigators ploughing
historical fields, and the vast improvement in the means of research, academic historiography is
losing whatever influence it had on the shaping of the image of the past stamped in public
consciousness. Our collective memory is not molded by professors at universities but by diverse
"memory agents." Such agents shape the image of the past in accordance with the
exigencies and pains of the present, projecting that image back into historical work. In our
information age, the print media, novels, lyrics of pop music, films, and television have a far
greater capacity to mold the image of the past than the circumspect discourse of well-documented
historical research.

Indeed, some could contend that this is the way it has always been: the history of the previous two
centuries is a web of narratives composed of national and political myths (socialist, or otherwise
fascist) that fashioned images of the world and of a national or class past. In accordance with those
images, a collective memory was forged. This perspective can also be applied to Zionist history:
the Zionist movement created a new Jewish collective memory based on the existence of a national
past in an ancestral territory, Erets Yisrael, on the age-old desire of the people to return to it, and
on the right of the Jews to a national existence in that land. It also created a whole pantheon of
heroes and warriors, imbuing Jewish history with a totally new meaning and direction, particularly
regarding the Diaspora. By their historical writings, Yehezkel Kaufman, Benzion Dinur, Joseph
Klausner, and Raphael Mahler also wished to shape a certain historical memory, each in
accordance with his political convictions.

Moreover, the secondary role of "professional" historians in
comparison with other agents of collective memory has long been a familiar phenomenon. Ahad
Ha'am cast the historical consciousness of generations of his disciples more than any
"certified" historian; this is also true of the writers Micah Joseph Berdyeczewski and
Joseph Hayyim Brenner as well as the political leaders Berl Katznelson and Yitshak Tabenkin.
One might indeed wonder whether there is really anything new today in collective memory. What
has changed to warrant another examination of the phenomenon? In past eras, the molding of
historical memory was controlled by a relatively small group of shapers of public opinion; what
was cherished in memory was largely the product of choices (conscious or not) made by the
leading political, social, or cultural elites. Today, however, public opinion is shaped by an anarchic
process in which elites and counter-elites have a share, along with diffuse, virtually fortuitous
forces that have the power, without any specific purpose or intention, to awaken public awareness and to implant within it images of the past. The loss of control over collective memory that we witness today can be interpreted as part of a process of democratization in whose course dominant, agenda-setting elites forfeited their central role in shaping collective memory, supplanted by other forces that were hitherto relatively silent in historical documentation.

It is also possible to see this in another light: as a process in which the image of memory loses its link with historical reality. Since the collective memory that is precipitated in the process is the corner stone of national identity, one can view the increasing gap between collective memory and historical research as providing the matrix for the creation of new myths.

The battle fought in Latrun on May 25, 1948--a confrontation known in Israeli military annals as Operation Bin-Nun A--illustrates the growing gap between collective memory and the body of facts established by historical research. Israel's War of Independence was the fundamental event in the history of Israeli nationalism, a "foundation myth." For that reason, its image in general memory--and even more, the changes in that image over the course of time--are of central importance for understanding national identity. The image of the battle of Latrun in Israeli collective memory reflects the dynamic process through which this event was appropriated by changing social groups. It also reflects the marginality of historical research in inducing this process.

The Chronicle of Events

Latrun was a small Arab village; located nearby was a large, fortified police station overlooking the plain of Ayalon. The plain of Ayalon is located halfway between the coastal plain and Jerusalem, and it is a famous battleground from the days of antiquity. During the Mandate, a vital road between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem passed through Latrun, in effect the only road linking Jerusalem, where the majority were Jewish, with the rest of the Jewish settlement--the 
yishuv
--in Palestine.

After the Arabs rejected the U.N. General Assembly decision on November 29, 1947, to partition Palestine into two states--one Jewish, one Arab--the Arabs swung into action against the Jews. Most of those attacks were concentrated on traffic moving between Jewish settlements. In February and March 1948, the Arab offensive reached its peak, and Jerusalem, to which the road ran through a narrow wadi between hills nestling Arab villages, was effectively cut off from the coastal plain. Following the British pullout from Palestine on May 15, several units of the Arab Legion that had been under British command seized the police station building near Latrun on May 17. They then had a commanding view of the road and prevented all traffic from moving between Jerusalem and the coastal plain. Jewish forces attempted to take the strategic site and clear a path to besieged Jerusalem, but these efforts failed. Finally an alternative road was forged, southwest of Latrun, and that new artery carried traffic to Jerusalem until 1967. In the course of the War of Independence, six battles were fought for Latrun, and 168 Israelis lost their lives there.

Leading up to the first battle of Latrun, the Israeli military high command received alarming messages in May 1948 from the leaders of Jerusalem describing the situation in the city as desperate: there was no food, ammunition, electricity, or water; they claimed they could only hold out for about another week or two.
1

Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion ordered Yigael Yadin, the operations officer and deputy chief of staff, to concentrate troop strength in order to breach a road to Jerusalem. The only reserve force at the disposal of the general staff was a contingent being formed precisely at that time, the Seventh Brigade. This unit was made up of soldiers who were called to military service by a mobilization order effective May 15. It comprised two regular battalions (the 71st and 72nd) and one armored battalion (the 73rd). Most of its officers had served in World War II in the British army, among them Shlomoh Shamir, head of the brigade, and Hayyim Laskov, commander of the armored battalion. The mid-level and lower echelons of officers in the brigade were drawn largely from instructors at the Israeli Training Department, which was terminated due to the shortage of manpower. The soldiers in this brigade were a mix of veteran soldiers and 500 new recruits; most of the latter were natives of the 
yishuv
 or had lived there for some years, but about 140 men were immigrants who had just arrived May 14 on the 
Teti
 (in Tel Aviv) and the 
Argentina
 (in Haifa) from Europe. There were no immigrants from Cyprus during this period.
2
 After disembarking, the fresh immigrants were transferred directly to the recruit reception center, where they were inducted. During the few days between their landing in Palestine and their arrival at the base of the Seventh Brigade in Hulda, they received some training in handling weapons and were even given firing practice on a genuine range, no small matter in those days. These immigrants were absorbed into the 72nd Battalion, A and B Companies. In keeping with standing practice in the British army, Israeli leaders kept an exact roll of personnel in the Seventh Brigade and updated changes in personnel strength from week to week.
3

As pressure mounted on Ben-Gurion from Jerusalem, the more he pressured Yadin to open the road to the city by capturing the Latrun area. In light of the inexperience of the Seventh Brigade, Yadin ordered the Alexandroni Brigade to transfer a battalion, the 32nd, to beef up the striking capacity of the force designated to capture the Latrun police station. That battalion was considered to be one of the most experienced in the Israeli Defense Force (IDF); it consisted mainly of young men from the agricultural colonies in the Sharon, well trained and familiar with the climate and the fighting conditions.

Although battalions and companies existed on paper, the brigade as a fighting force was not yet operational: equipment had just begun to arrive in Palestine, and the artillery pieces were not in working order or targeted at proper range. The machine guns were still packed in protective vaseline, and the soldiers did not know how to fire them. All soldiers had been issued rifles, but not everyone was in uniform. Only about a quarter of the men in the 32nd Battalion had canteens, and the men of the 72nd Battalion of the Seventh Brigade had only a small number of water canteens; they tried to improvise by using bottles of water. The recruits were not familiar with their individual equipment. All of this was added to the fact that the soldiers and officers in the 72nd Battalion knew one another only superficially, at best. The brigade lacked the time to consolidate itself militarily, in organizational terms and in respect to command structure.
4

Ben-Gurion ordered the army to attack the Latrun police station on the night of May 23. A bitter dispute erupted between Ben-Gurion and Yadin, who did not share Ben-Gurion's view that the situation in Jerusalem was critical; he wanted to postpone the attack by a week or ten days to allow the Seventh Brigade to prepare properly for the assault. Shamir also tried to convince Ben-Gurion to put off the attack two more days. After much dissension, Yadin and Shamir succeeded in persuading Ben-Gurion to delay the attack just 24 hours.

The attack commenced shortly before dawn on May 25. Two companies from the 32nd Battalion--A and B, totaling about 180 men--were ordered first to take the village of Latrun from the north, and then to attack the police station. B and C Companies from the 72nd Battalion, over 200 men, were also deployed. The mission of C Company was to block the road Hartuv-Shaar ha-Gai to prevent Arab reinforcements from reaching Latrun, while B Company was dispatched to capture Deir Ayyub in order to secure the line of advance of the 32nd Battalion.
5

B Company of the 32nd Battalion was pinned down in extremely heavy crossfire, and by the end of the day it had ceased to exist: casualties were 48 dead and 46 wounded (34 with light wounds, including those suffering from heatstroke); 6 had been taken prisoner. A Company succeeded in taking over high ground (Hill 314.2) and from this position was able to defend the retreat routes from the field of battle; it thus played a vital role in assisting the evacuation of the wounded and dead of the two battalions.
6

From the moment it took up field position, the 72nd Battalion was under heavy artillery bombardment. Its two commanders were wounded almost immediately, and most of the officers were also hit. By dawn the soldiers were pinned down in the cornfield at the foot of Latrun, exposed to the enemy. During the morning and afternoon of May 25, without officers and under heavy fire, the men were forced to find their way back to Beit Jiz, where army vehicles were supposed to be waiting for them. In fact, Beit Jiz had been evacuated by the IDF during the early afternoon, and those who arrived later were forced to continue on their own for another six kilometers to the Huldah-Latrun road; buses and even private cars were assembled there to pick up and evacuate the forces.

That day, the 72nd Battalion lost 23 men; 15 from B Company, 4 from C Company, 2 from the auxiliary company, and 2 from D Company. Forty-six were wounded; of these, 32 had light wounds (including those with heatstroke). Eight of the dead were new immigrants, all from B Company. According to another version, there were 20 killed and 140 wounded.
7

The weather that late May day was oppressive, a withering hamsin. The combatants suffered enormously from the heat and dryness. The descriptions of the battle emphasize the lack of water, which caused a number of soldiers to faint; others suffered heat exhaustion, and still others showed signs of extreme apathy and fatigue to the point where they lost their very instinct for survival. There were no reported differences between the newcomers and the native sons of Palestine, though it is reasonable to assume that the hamsin caused greater difficulties among the new immigrants. A large proportion of those counted as "light injuries" were suffering exhaustion due to the extreme heat, and most of these returned to their units within a week or two. Rabbi Shlomoh Goren, who attempted to locate the bodies of the missing and bring them to burial in 1949, reported that the majority of the dead lost their lives as a result of shelling and gunfire.
8

The trauma of defeat and hasty retreat was aggravated by the fact that they had to leave behind dead and even wounded, most of whom were then killed by Arab forces. This battle claimed more casualties than any other previous clash: 71 (or, according to another version, 72) men perished. For the first few days following the battle, until it had become clear that some of the missing were in hospital or had returned to their homes, there was a pervading impression that the catastrophe had been even worse. In any event, B Company of the 32nd Battalion and B Company of the 72nd Battalion had ceased to exist as fighting units. After the battle, the Arab Legion sent reinforcements to Latrun in the form of one battalion transferred from Jerusalem.

The "Official Version" of Events

In the contest for collective memory and the first historical description of a key event, there are clear advantages for the governing elite: it controls the media, supplies news to the papers, and has access to documents and testimony. In the struggle over forming the image of Latrun in Israeli national memory, the first battle was fought along lines drawn by Ben-Gurion and his followers.

In the month after Operation Bin-Nun A, newspapers carried only sparse reports about the confrontation. Most of the information came from foreign news agencies.
9
 Starting on May 26, 1948, the papers reported battles near Latrun but gave few details on what had occurred. On the Arab side, the Arab Legion claimed a great victory and 800 Jewish dead  (
Maariv
, May 27). Foreign sources reported that this had been the largest battle up to that time in Palestine (
Maariv
, May 28).
10

Israel remained silent until May 30, when the IDF staff spokesman announced the capture of Beit Jiz and Beit Susin (two villages south of the road to Jerusalem). In a briefing given to foreign journalists, a military spokesman stated that "the situation in Latrun is satisfactory."
11

On June 1, a new line made its appearance in the press: "The main aim is not to take Latrun but to deal a blow to the Legion" was the headline of 
Maariv
. The general gist was that, though Latrun had not been seized, the Legion had been weakened and the initiative now lay in Jewish hands.
12
 The Israelis also released figures on casualties: the Arabs had lost 250 men in the first eight days of battle, while Jewish losses "have not yet been finally determined, though from what is known, ten were killed and twenty wounded, while another twenty suffered extremely light injuries." This was the first official statement on losses in Operation Bin-Nun A.
13

On the eve of the first cease-fire (June 11), reports continued to flow in from the front at Latrun, which according to the assessment of foreign journalists was the only theater of operations in Palestine that resembled a traditional European battlefield. These reports indulged in huge exaggerations regarding the numbers of combatants on both sides: an Associated Press writer reported that there were 3,000 men on each side.
14
 A few days later, emphasis shifted to describing operations aimed at clearing the Burma Road, which was opened up "under the cover of the actions at Latrun" (
Haaretz
, June 14). From then on, the battles for Latrun were mentioned in the same breath as the opening of the Burma Road.

The Israeli "official version" was worked out by Ben-Gurion, who claimed that the battle for Latrun had been a military victory. In his analysis of political and military operations during "the month of fighting" presented to the provisionary State Council, he stressed the positive aspects of the battle for Latrun and even praised the performance of the Seventh Brigade. No other brigade of the IDF was singled out for special mention in that speech.
15
 Ben-Gurion's interpretation of the battle was confirmed during a debate with Yadin on July 3 before the so-called Commission of Five (a commission of ministers set up to investigate Ben-Gurion's allegations of a "political revolt" within the army general staff). In reponse to Yadin's claim that "the operation had ended in a terrible catastrophe," Ben-Gurion responded: "In my view, it was a great victory, though it did not come cheap."
16

The first direct, albeit partial, information on the battle was published in the journal 
Maarakhot
.
17
 This is the story of the battle from the perspective of the 32nd Battalion (Alexandroni Brigade), as told by the platoon and company commanders and by two additional combatants. The description is highly authentic, and all subsequent descriptions in the press and historical research are based on this review. It stresses the disastrous effect of the hamsin, the apathy of the soldiers as they went out to battle, and the enormous efforts of A Company in evacuating the wounded and providing cover to pull out soldiers of B Company and of the 72nd Battalion. It also describes the disappointment of the men who arrived in Beit Jiz and found no IDF forces there, and the necessity to leave some of the wounded in the village to be picked up later. There is mention of the entry of Arab forces into Beit Jiz as the IDF rearguard pulled out and headed for the Hulda road, and hints at the massacre of the wounded. The article presents data as reported by the participants without any editorial comment, explanations, or editing. Concentrating on questions of performance under fire, it does not touch on sensitive points in the battle for Latrun, except the abandonment of Beit Jiz. The article contains no calculations on total losses.

The most serious attempt to propagate the "official version" of the battle for Latrun was undertaken by Yisrael Ber in 1955. Lieutenant Colonel Ber had been Yadin's subordinate in the Planning Branch, Department of Operations, during the War of Independence. At that time, he had shared in Yadin's vehement criticism of Ben-Gurion's intervention in connection with the Seventh Brigade in Latrun. But over the seven following years, Ber changed his tune, becoming one of the most adept explicators of the Ben-Gurionian version of events. His work on Latrun remains the most solid and cogent material written on the topic to date. Ber attempts to focus on the events from a historical perspective, evaluating the results of the battles from both political and military points of view.
18

Early in his description of the background to the war, Ber is quick to stress the singular importance of Jerusalem, not just in terms of public morale but also militarily. It was a "strategic advance guard that helped cover the firm base, attracting enemy forces and diverting them from that base." In other words, the attacks on Jerusalem tied Arab forces down and prevented them from attacking Jewish population centers in the coastal plain, mainly in Tel Aviv.
19
 He makes allowances for the Seventh Brigade, maintaining that the unit had been obliged to mix together men from heterogeneous backgrounds in its ranks and did not have the time necessary for proper organization, but that there was no other choice. According to Ber, the Seventh Brigade was an outstanding example of a military force formed during the course of battle, losing its former identity as a militia and adopting the patterns of a regular army. He presents the command of the brigade in a highly favorable light, particularly the veterans of the British army. His depiction of the veterans of the Palmah and Haganah (elite clandestine, irregular forces) is less complimentary but still positive. Ber also comments favorably on the new immigrants but underscores their inadequate training; he describes the shortcomings of their equipment and weapons, and noted: "In our 'special' war . . . it was necessary to deploy our force as it was, to confront the enemy as it was."
20
 Indirectly, he accuses the Operations Department (mainly Yadin) of a failure in intelligence regarding the presence of the Arab Legion in Latrun on the eve of the battle: it was erroneously assumed that only a force of irregulars was stationed there, and thus no preparations had been made for an encounter with a regular army.

Ber also presents the first governmental figures on Israeli casualties: 75 dead, among them 50 men from the 32nd Battalion of the Alexandroni Brigade and 25 men from the 72nd Battalion of the Seventh Brigade--data that closely match the findings of much later research on the battles. He makes no reference to the number of casualties among the new immigrants.

Ber depicts the events at Latrun as a heroic epic, such as occurs when nations are born or when there is an historical breakthrough by a national movement of liberation. He formulates the essential conclusion to be drawn from the clashes at Latrun as the "dialectical law operative in warfare": though the tactical achievements at the beginning of the war on the Jerusalem front did not guarantee the security of the city and protect the access route to it, the three tactical failures in Latrun nonetheless did secure the supply route to Jerusalem (the Burma Road) and help divert forces of the Arab Legion away from Jerusalem. According to Ber, the dialectical inversion (defeat that is in effect victory) derived from the secret of strategic understanding of the situation by the supreme commander, Ben-Gurion: he was able to identify the key elements and to subordinate the necessarily limited tactical considerations of the army command to this broader perspective. Ben-Gurion could not have found a more capable advocate than Ber, who points out all the deficiencies and faults of the command, the brigade, the tactics, and the equipment but blames them on the special situation: the birth of a state and the concomitant emergence of a fighting force from the underground.

Ben-Gurion adhered to this version all of his life. Commenting in 1950 on the Latrun campaign, he once again underscored the suffering of Jerusalem under siege during the month of battle after May 15, and he noted: "We set up a new brigade then--the Seventh. It was made up of immigrants from Cyprus who had just come to Israel . . . . Not a single battalion of the regular troops in that brigade was trained, and based on the established rules of warfare, it should have been forbidden to send them to the front. Yet Jerusalem was in mortal danger, there was no choice. . . . Latrun was not conquered--but Jerusalem was saved."
21
 In 1973, shortly before his death, Ben-Gurion was invited to a gathering of the veterans of the Seventh Brigade. Due to his declining health, he chose instead to send them a message with his felicitations, a letter in which he repeated his earlier statements. The elements of "Jerusalem in danger," "no choice," and "defeat that is victory" transformed the battle for Latrun into a myth, imbuing the bloodletting there with transcendent meaning and value.

The "Other Version" of the Palmah

Latrun was not the only defeat in the War of Independence, and Operation Bin-Nun A was not its bloodiest failure. The battle fought by the Alexandroni Brigade for the strongholds in Iraq al-Manshiyya on December 28, 1948, cost 88 fatalities. There had been 78 killed in the medical convoy dispatched to Hadassah Hospital on Mt. Scopus on April 13, 1948. In the battle for Jenin on June 3 that year, the Carmeli Brigade had lost 50 men. Fatalities in the fight for Gush Etsyon were far heavier (157 dead in the last battle on May 13).
22
  Yet none of these events were later associated with the chain of rumors, stories, and controversy over the decades like Operation Bin-Nun A. Indeed, as a result of that battle, Latrun became a milestone in the annals of the birth of the state. One of the explanations for the unique place given to this defeat was that for 19 years after the battle, until the Six-Day War, Latrun continued to dominate the road to Jerusalem, forcing Israelis to detour around it--a kind of constant, troubling memento to past mistakes. But the lack of a liberating catharsis of victory following on the heels of trauma was not peculiar to Latrun: Gush Etsyon likewise did not return to Israeli control until after 1967, and the same applies to Jenin and the road to Mt. Scopus. The question why a certain event becomes the focus of intense public attention to the point where it is mythicized, while another is largely forgotten, deserves special investigation. It seems to me that Latrun's centrality in public memory and in historiography on the War of Independence can be attributed to the fact that this battle became a focal point of heated contention and head-on struggle between two elite groups: Ben-Gurion and the veterans of the British army on one side, and the leaders of the Haganah and Palmah (including Yadin) on the other. These were two elites of the 
yishuv
 that remained in control in the early phase of the state. The Palmah and Haganah veterans felt threatened by the radical changes that had occurred in the army with the transition from the Haganah to the IDF.

The struggle between the two elites began with the question of how the army should be structured and was later extended to the shaping of the collective memory of the War of Independence. Latrun was both cynosure and symbol. The outlines of this clash were clear even before Operation Bin-Nun A and became more pronounced in its wake. Ben-Gurion's attempts to pressure Yadin and force him to accept his views on what Yadin saw as an operational matter generated considerable outrage. It was one of many actions by Ben-Gurion that clearly reflected his view that Haganah and Palmah veterans were inferior to those of the British army when it came to their military knowledge and training.
23
 The fact that the high command of the Seventh Brigade was composed of veterans of the British army, headed by Shlomoh Shamir and Hayyim Laskov, made the unit a matter of heated controversy in the dispute between the two elites. Shamir's failure to stand up to Ben-Gurion when he ordered an attack on the night of May 23, as well as Shamir's acceptance of the defense minister's judgment and of the dangers associated with the attack, were interpreted by Yadin and his associates as a negative example of British army tradition: the obedience of orders without protest. They interpreted the readiness to attack in a frontal assault, and especially during the day, as examples of an attitude that viewed losses too lightly.

The "official version" of events as touted by Ben-Gurion and the veterans of the British army disregarded the operative and tactical details of the campaign, foregrounding instead the strategic conception and the role of the events at Latrun in the rescue of Jerusalem. The "other version," espoused by Yadin and men of the Haganah and Palmah, concentrated on the details of the operation's implementation. Yadin's basic argument was that the brigade had been sent to a predestined defeat because the unit was unprepared for combat. Thus, not only did the operation fail to open the route to Jerusalem, but the sole force that might have later been able to effect a successful breakthrough--if the operation had been prudently postponed another week or two--was destroyed at Latrun. At the heart of the "other version" was an array of disturbing issues: the defective equipment of the soliders and their unfamiliarity with it; the lack of water canteens; the delay in launching the attack; the absence of intelligence; the negligible involvement of the brigade command in the course of the battle; the failure to deploy the reserve battalion during the confrontation; the limited intervention on the part of the armored battalion; the small amount of assistance provided by artillery; the inability to secure routes for withdrawal; and the failure to supply water and transport for the retreating soldiers. Against the claim of 
ein brerah
 (no choice), the dissenters raised the allegation of "criminal negligence." Counterposed to the glorification of those who sacrificed their lives and the significance of their death was the claim that these losses had been useless, that these men had died in vain.

The question of the participation of new immigrants in the battle was first broached in the framework of this dispute. In his testimony before the Commission of Five, Yadin described the state of the Seventh Brigade on the eve of battle. As far as the degree of their preparedness was concerned, he noted that the men "were all green recruits." After pointing out that "based on all military considerations, the action should not have been carried out, and it resulted in a terrible catastrophe," he recounted what had occurred on the battlefield:

A battalion that had been given three days basic training was sent into battle, and men fell mortally wounded, the safety-latches on their rifles still locked. . . . They went straight from the boat to the recruitment center. There were more casualties that day than in any previous operation.
24

Yadin's emphasis on the inexperience of the battalion, on the fact that it was composed of new immigrants, and on the extent of the casualties were meant to underscore his contention that the brigade had not been combat-ready and that Ben-Gurion's intervention had contravened all the rules of military logic. The component of newly arrived immigrants added a touch of drama to the arguments put forward by Yadin and increased the impression that there had been a lack of responsibility on the part of those who had decided to send the unit into battle.

As noted above, the press reported sparingly on the battle at Latrun. Only between the lines was it possible to discern the fact that there were new immigrants in the ranks of the recently formed brigade.
25
 Yet rumors about Latrun soon began to circulate within both the army and the general public. An article in 
Davar
 (June 18, 1948) enumerates the deficiencies in the army. Among these the author stresses two questions that apparently stemmed from the Latrun battle: why were the soldiers not provided with water canteens, and why were they not given identification tags? In a diary entry at the beginning of June by Hadasah Avigdori-Avidov, a Palmah soldier, there is a description of a meeting between immigrant soldiers, known as Gahal (shorthand for 
giyus huts la-arets
). She remarks: "They also say that the fighting forces in the Latrun area are composed mainly of Gahal men. . . . Poor guys, they sent them right straight into that hell."
26
 A book by Uri Avneri, published shortly after the end of the war, contains a story about a new immigrant from Poland: during the retreat from Latrun, "a whole canteen full of water was needed to douse his face, mouth, ears, and nose in order to revive him and induce him to save his own life."
27
 In one of the best-known theatrical pieces of the era, "Be-arvot ha-Negev" ("In the Wilderness of the Negev") by Yigal Mosinsohn, one of the protagonists exclaims:

I was in Latrun! Look, I don't know if that name says very much to you. But man, that was hell on earth, Latrun! And there too, I had recruits from abroad. Not only weren't there enough weapons--there weren't any water canteens either. And then the hamsin, and those flies--the men fainted in the field, fainted and died out there in the field . . . and the order handed down was cruel: to go on! To go on at any price! To open up the route to Jerusalem--otherwise Jewish Jerusalem would be obliterated! And I'll never forget one of the new immigrants who was lying there on the ground, he was in the throes of death. He'd asked to speak with me, his commander. The smile of a dying man! He said to me: "Better . . . here! It's better here! Take care of my mother." Then he died. Nobody knows where his mother is. . . . To go through everything--and then to be killed in Erets Yisrael!
28

The issue of Latrun was drawn into the conflict between Ben-Gurion and the Palmah. It served to call into question Ben-Gurion's moral authority and the prudence of his judgments, and it damaged his credibility as a leader. Because the ruling elite had control over access to the media, the "other version" was forced to use alternative channels: rumor, word of mouth, conversations around campfires and in the tents of the soldiers, and at reunions of former combatants. Belles lettres played a significant role in communicating the message, since literature was not affected by the censorship or limitations to which men in the military were subject. There were two essential features in the rumors circulated: the extent of the casualties suffered, and the large percentage of new immigrants among them. As the story spread, these two elements were increasingly emphasized. What gave these rumors credibility was the fact that many of the soldiers who had fallen in Latrun were not given a proper burial until after the war, in a special operation carried out by Rabbi Goren in cooperation with the Jordanians. Given those circumstances, it was natural that there were stories about unidentified dead.
29

Ben-Gurion himself helped to lend credibility to that version. In his 1950 speech, he not only recounted (erroneously) that the Seventh Brigade was made up of immigrants from Cyprus, but he also stated that "more than half its men were killed or wounded in the bloody battles."
30
 The exaggeration in depicting the role of the new immigrants in the brigade and the percentage of casualties served to explain the failure of the attack on Latrun and to enhance the fame and glory of his preferred brigade. In this way, however, he also bolstered the "other version" and strengthened the arguments advanced by its critics regarding the lack of responsibility he had demonstrated in his military reasoning.

So long as Ben-Gurion served as both prime minister and defense minister, criticism on Latrun was restricted to the realms of hearsay and fiction. The writings of Ber were the sole historical version available. Yadin never forgave his former subordinate for his treachery (as he saw it) when Ber switched sides and became Ben-Gurion's favored historian and close associate. Yadin did not conceal his gleeful satisfaction when it was discovered that Ber had been a Soviet agent.
31

In 1964, the dispute over Latrun finally erupted onto the pages of the press. Within the framework of trying to magnify the public image of Moshe Dayan, Ben-Gurion's protégé at the time, Ben-Gurion stated that if Dayan had been chief of staff during the War of Independence, the situation would have ended differently. In reaction to this remark, generals in that war began to circulate their criticisms of Ben-Gurion's actions at the time as supreme commander. For the first time, Yadin publicly accused Ben-Gurion of being responsible for the debacle of Bin-Nun A. In response, three veterans of the British army and ardent disciples of Ben-Gurion--Shamir, Laskov, and Fritz Eshet--gave a detailed interview on Latrun that appeared in the press on the eve of Independence Day 1964. They justified Ben-Gurion's position, using phraseology coined by Ber, and criticized the general staff. They also complained about the way the Palmah and Haganah were inciting accusations against the Seventh Brigade and Ben-Gurion. There was a clear denial of the rumors regarding the hundreds of dead ("in the three battles for Latrun--including the operations to open the Burma Road--there were a total of 135 fatalities--and more than 75% of those killed were natives of Palestine"). Those killed had not fallen as "cannon fodder"--an expression that will return in this connection--but had died in a courageous battle.
32
 At this stage, the initiative was still in the hands of Ben-Gurion and his supporters.

Only in 1967 did the pendulum start to swing the other way. In the special section of 
Maariv
 for Independence Day--one day before Israeli reality was forever altered--an interview with Yadin appeared for the first time. Ben-Gurion was already out in the political desert, and Levi Eshkol was prime minister and minister of defense. Yadin now allowed himself a leisurely review of his relations with Ben-Gurion. The battle for Latrun was among the various operations he commented on; he mentioned the new immigrants and, in response to a question regarding losses, stated that hundreds had died in the battles for Latrun. In so doing, he strengthened the credibility of the rumors regarding the extent of losses. But that was not his main point. He recalled the matter only as an illustration of Ben-Gurion's misjudgment about Jerusalem, a mistaken view that had caused him to abandon military logic and to make a serious error.
33

In the wake of the Six-Day War, a wave of new articles were published on Latrun. In this context of renewed interest, the journalist Uri Oren invited the commanders and senior officers of both battles (Bin-Nun A and B) to gather together and confer in Latrun. The results of that discussion were published in two fascinating articles, though the positions elaborated there provided nothing new in respect to the two familiar versions. Shamir stated his position frankly: "Even if I had known right from the start that the battle was lost, I'd still have gone ahead" because "one battle is not the war . . . and winning the war--that's the objective." All the other commanders, except for Laskov, were of the opinion that Latrun was a battle that should not have taken place; it had not achieved its aim and had exacted a bloody toll.

Parallel with this, Uri Oren carried out a kind of survey among his friends regarding losses at Latrun. The estimates he was given ranged between 500 and 700 dead. One of his respondents even thought casualties were much higher, between 1,000 and 2,000 killed. Oren noted that, in the two Bin-Nun battles, no more than several hundred combatants had taken part; of these, 120 had been killed and many wounded. In this discussion, the issue of the new immigrants was hardly broached.
34

The Six-Day War generated considerable interest among foreign journalists in Israel and its military exploits, including the War of Independence. The first token of this renewed interest was Jon and David Kimchi's 
Both Sides of the Hill
, followed by the bestseller by Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre, 
O, Jerusalem
, and a book by Dan Kurzman, 
Genesis 1948
.
35
 The Kimchi book was the most credible of the three, 
O, Jerusalem
 the most popular. Kurzman's book was discussed in a lengthy article in  
Yediot Aharonot
 that also touched on the campaign at Latrun. In a reference to Bin-Nun A, the article stated that 140 were killed in the battle, with hundreds wounded and scores of missing.
36

This article led to a response by Aryeh Yitshaki, who claimed that Kurzman had represented the position espoused by Shamir and his associates and had slandered the Palmah. He also emphatically rejected Kurzman's figures on the number of fatalities, asserting that 74 soldiers had died in Bin-Nun A and 6 were taken prisoner.
37
 Over the next decade, Yitshaki came to have a virtual monopoly on research on Latrun. His detailed study on Latrun was brought out in 1982, based on documents from the IDF Archives and debriefings of the IDF Historical Department.

The reunion of Seventh Brigade veterans on August 29, 1973, in Latrun was the opportunity for additional reviews and remarks on the events that had transpired there, including comments by Shamir and Laskov, felicitations from Ben-Gurion, and responses by Yitshaki. The figures given by Shamir regarding losses in the battle put the total number of dead in Bin-Nun A and B and the struggle for the Burma Road at 137. He stressed that 50 of those killed were from the battalion composed of men born in Palestine (the 32nd). The figures published by Yitshaki were quite similar to those of Shamir: Yitshaki noted that in the Seventh Brigade there were only about 600 new immigrants out of a total of 2,200 men, and that aside from the 72nd Battalion, which had some new immigrants, the battalions consisted in the main of long-time immigrants and natives of Palestine. He confirmed that most of the losses in Bin-Nun A had been suffered by the 32nd. When Ben-Gurion and his supporters emphasized the lack of military experience of the new immigrants, Yitshaki leaped to their defense: "It's easy enough to blame defeat on the new immigrants, yet the real reasons for that [defeat] lie elsewhere." He noted that the newcomers did have some military background, since he believed they had been given basic training in Cyprus and their morale was high. He blamed the defeat on Ben-Gurion and his panic regarding Jerusalem, and on errors made in the operational and tactical sphere by the brigade command. In Yitshaki's analysis, Latrun was the greatest defeat ever suffered by the IDF.
38

One might have expected that, after a consensus was reached among the two leading camps regarding the number of fatalities, this issue would no longer have been a matter of controversy. However, totally different statistics continued to appear in the established press and were not denied. Writing in the daily 
Haaretz
 about the memorial monument at Latrun, Haviv Kenaan stated that, during the War of Independence, 430 Israeli soldiers had been killed in action on the Ayalon plain (by comparison, Yitshaki's figures were 168 slain). In a letter to the editor in response, Barukh Nadel contended that "on the basis of investigations I conducted in 1948 and later on," the number of those killed was roughly double the figure given by Kenaan. He claimed that in the first battle for Latrun, to which "survivors of the Holocaust" were sent, "armed with rifles they did not know how to fire . . . some 500 men had died in battle on that one day alone." He argued that Ben-Gurion wanted this defeat in order "to be able to create the myth of the 'invincible Arab Legion' and to justify the handing over (or abandoning) of the city of David to Abdullah."
39
 Speculations on the "collusion" between Ben-Gurion and Abdullah in the War of Independence were to feed numerous historical studies and myths.
40
 What is interesting here is the way that alleged collusion was linked to the issue of the number of dead and the question of new immigrants in the Latrun battle.

In the late 1970s and 1980s, articles appeared expounding the versions of either Shamir or Yitshaki, stressing the established facts regarding battlefield losses in Bin-Nun A. The number of fatalities according to both versions ranged between 71 and 75.
41
 Nonetheless, these frequent references to the actual number killed in battle did not penetrate into collective memory. In a debate in the Knesset on November 18, 1985, Knesset member Uzi Landau touched on the battle at Latrun, citing a staggering casualty figure: 2,000 dead. After others countered that this was a gross exaggeration, especially given that the number of fatalities for the entire war was 6,000, Landau backtracked. He was ready to accept a compromise figure of 1,000 dead at Latrun, but no fewer.
42
 In the wake of these exchanges, accurate facts were published once again in the press, but the public image of the number of dead at Latrun remained a mythologized quantity.

The frequent references to the losses and the new immigrants were intended to exemplify and explain the interpretations offered by the two 
yishuv
 elites and their followers regarding Latrun. The more time passed, the more the dispute forfeited its relevance and concrete meaning, becoming a debate on a historical issue in the War of Independence aimed at glorifying the role of the respective elites in the foundation myth of the state.

The Emergence of a New Elite and a Third Version

In the mid-1970s, another narrative of the battle at Latrun began to crystallize behind the lattice of the two existing versions. It did not claim to be based on archival materials, reports and protocols, articles, reviews by commanders, or assessments by historians. This narrative presented the battle--and, through the prism of that confrontation, the War of Independence as a whole--as it had come to be depicted over the years in the memory of those who had remained until then on the periphery of collective remembrance: the new immigrants.

Collective memory of such a fundamental event in the forging of Israeli identity like the War of Independence contains assumptions shared by the whole nation that require no proof and serve as the ideological foundation justifying the existence of the national entity. By participating in the collective memory, a feeling of shared experience by all parts of society is created. Thus, social groups that did not take part in (or felt excluded from) this formative experience look for a narrative through which they might link up with the collective memory as part of their struggle to gain recognition and legitimacy.

Several processes transformed the Israeli self-image and thus also modified emphases in national identity. The Six-Day War in 1967 and its immediate aftermath were the crowning point of the strong and heroic sabra, the fearless warrior, triumphant in victory, scornful of weakness and defeat. The symbolic figure of the nation at that juncture was Moshe Dayan. Then came the Yom Kipur War in 1973, which not only diminished the aura around Dayan but also raised questions about the validity of generally accepted truths in Israeli society. Israeli television aired shattering images of Israeli defeat, of soldiers being taken into captivity, and of weakness and fear. Israel after that war did not return to its sense of itself as a strong, invincible power. From the welter of anxieties generated by the war, powerful images of the Holocaust arose. After this watershed in consciousness, the Shoah ceased to be a past event incorporated only as a segment of the history of 
part
 of the nation; it now became an element of abiding presence in the collective memory of Israel. Israel's history was no longer presented as a tale in which all was light, crowned with ultimate success. It also became the story of those who had failed, a chronicle of the weak. As the axes of self-understanding shifted, the Holocaust survivor became one of the new foci in national memory and consciousness. Israel's birth was not just a saga of glorious warriors but also of uprooted Jews, harried refugees who had made it to Israel by the skin of their teeth, encountered there a hostile environment, and earned their right of place by bloody sacrifice on its battlefields.

This process of revision gained momentum with the ascendancy of Menahem Begin to the reins of state power. Whereas previous governments had largely been the heirs of the elites of the pre-state   
yishuv
, Begin belonged only marginally to the 
yishuv
. His government gave expression and a new sense of empowerment to everyone who felt disadvantaged or discriminated against when it came to his place in the old patterns of national memory: for example, Oriental Jews, new immigrants, and the "fighting family" (the Irgun underground, or IZL, the right wing underground connected with the Revisionist Party, which did not accept the authority of the 
yishuv
 and Haganah leadership). The fundamental critique of long-accepted elements of the collective memory and their remolding involved the entire history of Zionism, the narrative about the establishment of the state and its formative years, the role played by various Jewish communities in the national movement, the importance of diverse social and political groups in the struggle prior to the creation of the state, the processes of immigrant absorption, and the attitude of the  
yishuv
 to the destruction of European Jewry during the war and to the survivors in its aftermath. All of these issues were now placed at the top of the agenda of national remembrance and consciousness. The veteran elites of the 
yishuv
 and their inheritors within the Israeli left were put on the defensive. Although historical research looked on them with benevolence, emphasizing their achievements in establishing a Jewish entity in Palestine, it was not historiography that molded collective memory but rather those other "agents" of remembrance: politicians, the press, television, and literature. The emergence of new elites was accompanied by the construction of a new narrative of the past. That narrative was principally based on testimony by the living and was nourished by the claim that existing documentation did not accord them their proper place in history.

Latrun soon became the central myth of the Holocaust survivors who had participated in the War of Independence. What elements functioned to transform Latrun into the magnet for the frustrations of the immigrant survivors in the War of Independence on the one hand, and the focus for their integration into the collective memory of that war on the other? As mentioned, the leitmotiv of new immigrants had accompanied the Latrun story from its inception. There was a kernel of fact here (the companies of the 72nd Battalion, most of whose men were new immigrants) as well as a basis for the genesis of myth (the persistent lack of clarity regarding the actual number killed, the fact that dead were left behind on the battlefield, the confusion and uncertainty during retreat and defeat). These elements were compounded by the rumors that shaped the image of Latrun into the most bitter battle and worst defeat in the War of Independence. The battle of Latrun remained a focus of interest in the media, reexamined and rediscussed in each decade, within the framework of the dispute between Ben-Gurion and the Haganah, the British army and the Palmah over their respective place in the history of the war. It was the veterans of the Palmah who nourished the leitmotiv of the new immigrants, using it to blame the commanders of the operation for the fate of the newcomers.

Until recently, there has been little research on the participation of Holocaust survivors in the War for Independence. That lacuna is due principally to one encompassing historiographic fact: serious investigation on the War of Independence generally is still in its infancy. There have been at least three recent studies documenting the contribution of Shoah survivors to the war effort.
43
 Since each scholar has a different definition of "new immigrant" (those who immigrated from 1945 on, or in 1948, or after May 15, 1948), it is difficult to obtain uniform data. Nonetheless, it is clear that Holocaust survivors made up a significant segment of the soldiers, especially survivors who immigrated to Palestine 
before
 1948. According to calculations by Emanuel Sivan, the percentage of losses among that segment of the combatants was no less than that of the native sons of the 
yishuv
. By contrast, the number of killed and wounded among the 1948 immigrants was relatively small, since a substantial number did not arrive in Israel until after the critical period in the fighting in early June; thus, their period of exposure to combat was shorter.
44
 Based on accepted figures, the 1948 immigrants made up about one quarter of all soldiers (some 25,000) during the autumn and winter of 1948/49; according to one study, they even composed approximately one-third of the strength of the combat units.
45

The shorter the period the immigrant spent in Palestine before being conscripted and sent to the front, the stronger was his sense of alienation and the more deficient and difficult his social and psychological integration. Although the immigrants of 1945-1947 were more involved in combat operations and made greater personal sacrifices, they were also better prepared for action at the front and were able to integrate well into the fighting forces. The conscription of Gahal soldiers, carried out mainly after May 15, 1948, and with great haste, was traumatic. There are numerous descriptions of the difficulties of absorption and of the shortcomings of Israeli society grappling with the problems of immigrant absorption during a time of crisis and war.
46

It appears there was no other battle during the War of Independence in which the role of the new immigrants was so central to the chronicle of events. There were other battles during later phases of the war in which the immigrants played a greater part in the fighting, yet there was no battle in which the context of their participation was dramatized to the point that it became an integral component of the story as it took root in public memory. For that reason, when the soldiers of Gahal awakened to the importance of their place in the history of the War of Independence, the battle of Latrun lent itself as a natural focus.

At first, the immigrants only wished to make sure that collective memory would give them credit where credit was due: recording the importance of their contribution to that battle. They regarded the widespread tendency to present their lack of experience as one of the supposed factors underlying the defeat as an insult, a perspective that had contributed to a negative image of the immigrants in Israeli public opinion. The first expression of opposition was from an ex-soldier, Shlomoh Lieblich, in 1968. He denounced what he believed was an attempt by the commanders of the brigade to conceal their omissions and shortcomings by pointing an accusing finger at the new immigrants. 
47
 However, Lieblich himself had not been one of the new immigrants; his opposition was still within the bounds of the "other version" and expressed the bitterness felt by a segment of the soldiers toward the brigade command. The first public instance of a "new immigrant" viewpoint was in an interview given by Yehudah Deutsch to  
Maariv
.
48
 He recounted that he had arrived in Palestine on May 14, 1948, on the 
Argentina
. Deutsch emphasized that he and his comrades had had some military training and all had been given some instruction on handling weapons. It was important for him to dispel the widespread image of the immigrant as a soldier who collapsed under the stress of combat: the wretched conditions of the battle, particularly the dehydration as a result of heatstroke and the lack of canteens, were what led to the state of apathy. Deutsch noted: "It's simply not true that the immigrants fell apart right away, that they didn't demonstrate any fighting spirit," and countered: "what success did the other battalions have in that battle, units without any immigrants?"
49
 The aim of his protestation was modest: to secure for the immigrants their just place in the heroic narrative of the battle. Deutsch did not criticize the fact that immigrants were sent into the line of fire: "There was no one else." And he had no complaints about their lack of equipment: "There simply were no canteens. And nobody hid the ammunition. There just wasn't any." Deutsch did not look back in anger. Rather, he regarded the confrontation at Latrun from the perspective of a man who had found his place in the system and viewed his own past as an integral part of that fabric of national belonging. When responding 12 years later to Shamir's article in 
Maarakhot
, Deutsch stressed again that the difference in the level of training of the newcomers and the "local" recruits had been minimal, and that the heat and thirst had made no distinction between old immigrants and new.
50

The story of Hadasah Lampel, a member of the 73rd Battalion of the Palmah, should also be recalled in this connection. She served as signaler in the half-track that penetrated into the inner courtyard of the police building in Latrun in Battle Bin-Nun B. Lampel was put in command of the vehicle after its commander had been killed, and she reported, bravely and with cool-headed composure, on what was taking place until she was killed along with the rest of her men. Lampel was one of the "Children of Teheran," a group of children, most of them orphans, who came to Palestine through Iran in 1943. Her mother and sisters arrived in Israel four months after she had been killed in action. Although Lampel did not fit in the category of "new immigrant" in terms of the conventional definitions, she became a symbol of the bravery of that group. Her letters to her family reflected the experiences and problems of adjustment and absorption encountered by young immigrants: the change of her first name from "Halina" to "Hadasah"; her difficulties learning to write and think in Hebrew; the concern that tormented her regarding her relatives back in the Soviet Union; her need to excel and to become a source of pride for her family. All of these qualities identified her as a typical young survivor. The fact that members of her family did not succeed in immigrating to Israel until after she had fallen in battle, and their difficulties in establishing the circumstances of her death (problems that arose in part because of their lack of knowledge of Hebrew and their unfamiliarity with the country) integrated the Lampel story into the web of difficulties in absorption encountered by an immigrant family. Moreover, her act of valor under fire provided a legitimacy not only to her own family but also to all those who immigrated to Palestine after 1939 and had directly experienced the horrors of the Shoah.
51

Parallel with the approach that sought to integrate the immigrants within the saga of heroism of Latrun, another tendency emerged: Latrun as the focus for the disappointments and bitterness of the new immigrants. "I was Sent Straight to Latrun" was the title of an article on the Gahal recruits, a piece for which former Gahal members had been interviewed. The heading was a quote from Efraim Karni, who (reminiscent of the content of remarks by Yadin to the Commission of Five) noted: "Among my buddies were men killed while they were trying to pull the still locked trigger of their rifle. No one had explained to them, or they didn't understand the explanation in Hebrew, that in order to fire they first had to release the lock." Another commented: "They did not always take the men right from the ship to the front, but in the cases where that happened, it was wrong, it was a sin."
52

In these interviews, Latrun emerged as a drama of alienation and estrangement. The immigrants sent into battle were strangers in a strange land. They did not know its landscape and had no opportunity to see anything except what passed by the window of the bus transporting them to battle. They set out in the dark of night, not knowing where they were being taken or why. They did not know where to pull back to, what route to follow. They came as lonely, solitary individuals, often the sole survivors of their family or community. If they had any relatives in Israel, they were not allowed to contact them. A lack of communication was at the root of their encounter. Their language was unfamiliar to the commanders and fellow soldiers in the unit, and they were baffled by the Hebrew in which they were addressed. No one explained to them why they were embarking upon this attack. Nobody briefed them on what they should do. And when dawn came, they found themselves under a murderous hail of fire. The searing heat sapped their strength, and the bites of the mosquitos drove them to distraction. An alien place and alien people, terror and enmity--and a debilitating foreign heat. Latrun symbolized everything that was difficult, strange, and alienating in the course of absorption: the impersonal way in which they were treated, the obliteration of their previous identities, the disregard of the past trauma they had suffered, the arrogant attitude of the natives, a feeling of discrimination and deprivation, a sense of inferiority, and disappointment with the Jewish state that had not given them a sense of belonging, of being at home.
53
 Latrun became the emblem of their estrangement.

This then was the pattern of memory of the War of Independence as it was stamped in the remembrance of a segment of the survivors. The trauma of emigration and resettlement, uprooting and replanting, is always saturated with bitterness, disappointment, and pain: the new reality can never satisfy the expectations of those who have longed for its coming. All the more so when the immigrants facing absorption have gone through the ordeal they had had to endure during six years of war, and even after liberation, being shunted from camp to camp, homeless wanderers.

Coming to Israel was simultaneously a catharsis of liberation and the genesis of new trauma. The demand, overt or covert, to assimilate to the dominant culture, manners, and social norms in Israel as a precondition for absorption was accepted by the majority of the immigrants without protest. Over the course of many years, they internalized those expectations to the best of their ability. Only after the lengthy process of absorption was completed, and they had become an integral part of Israeli society--only after those same norms they had tried so hard to embrace in their youth began to crumble with the decline of the old elites of the 
yishuv
, and after other ethnic groups, especially Oriental Jews, clamored for their right to be Israelis while retaining a special cultural identity, thus replacing the concept of "the melting pot" with a more pluralistic notion of what was accepted as a legitimate Israeli identity--only then did the feelings of alienation and estrangement that had been suppressed by them over the decades reemerge into consciousness. The survivors began to give testimony on their experiences during the Holocaust and during absorption. When they did, they found the outlines of their own past in the myth of Latrun that had already taken root in collective memory. The story recounted until then by the elite veterans was appropriated by the immigrants, and now became their own claim to glory.
54

Just as the orchards of Petah Tikvah came to symbolize the covenant with the land of Palestine for members of the Second Aliyah, as work on the highways became the symbolic experience for the Third Aliyah, and as the years of the 
maabarot
, the transit camps, and the building of development towns were symbolic for the Oriental Jews, Latrun now served the Shoah survivors as a symbol of their role in the central myth of the establishment of the state, the War of Independence. It was not accidental that they demanded a symbol of commemoration similar to projects such as Yad La-banim, which various settlements had built to memorialize their sons who had fallen in the war. Whoever was not mentioned among the dead, whose name was not immortalized on a monument, had been deprived of his or her part in the collective memory of the war. The fact that no one commemorated the immigrant soldiers who had been slain, because "they were not anyone's sons or graduates,"
55
 deprived them, as it were, of any rights to the Israeli identity that was wrought in crucible of war, the brotherhood of the warriors of 1948. The demand for a presence in memory and concrete expressions of that presence was in reality a call for recognition of a new kind of Israeli identity: one that retained basic features of the old 
yishuv
 identity but also internalized a world of memory and experience of the survivors.

In the version of the new immigrants, the story of Latrun was not based on papers and documents but on the later testimony of those who felt they had played a vital part in those events. The definition of oral history as an attempt "to elaborate a counter-history--from the 'bottom up'--and to reconstruct the version of the 'conquered'--ethnic or cultural minorities, women or workers"
56
 is useful for delineating the character of the counter-history of Latrun. Here indeed is an anti-establishment counter-version: it is uninterested in issues that lay at the heart of the controversy between the two other competing versions. Its purpose is neither to destroy the foundations of the basic myth of the establishment of the state nor to challenge its existence, but rather to present a new pretender to participation in the saga. In the historical documentation, that pretender had hitherto been depicted as marginal and secondary, the object of action by others. It now demanded its rightful place of honor.

The Myth of Latrun and Deconstructionism

As this version of the Latrun myth developed, writers and poets also latched onto the story of Latrun, transforming it into a kind of battering ram for deconstruction of one of the basic mythologies of the state: Israel as the Ingatherer of the Exiles, the sanctuary for the survivors. Just as Latrun was part of the collective memory of the heroism and participation in the founding events of the state, it also became the basis for a collective memory of guilt--the indictment against a state born in transgression. The revision of the collective memory was perpetuated by these writers, members of the Israeli intelligentsia who belonged both to the generation of Palmah and to the first generation after the establishment of the state.

The first poet to deal with the Latrun affair was Natan Alterman. In his poem "Be-terem or"(Before Light), Alterman recounts the story of the Seventh Brigade, "the lamb in the battle for sacrifice." He writes about the "battle of those who disembarked from the ships." The most difficult question he poses is the matter of selection: why were those sent to face the fire of battle the refugees from Europe who had survived the war, while many of the members of the 
yishuv
 went on with their everyday lives?
57

Alterman's indictment was given little attention at the time. The accusation it contained, though it touched a painful nerve, was too general; it lacked a sharp anti-establishment barb. In the final analysis, Alterman integrated the disaster of the Seventh Brigade within the broader epic of the birth of the nation. "The force of the things revealed in the play" provides the death of the survivors with meaning and added value, even if it does not justify their being sent into the line of fire.

Some 25 years later, Aryeh Sivan recalled the memory of "the immi-grant Gahal soldiers who died in the fields of Latrun in the course of Operation Bin-Nun" (
Maariv
, May 8, 1981) in a poem that explores remembrance and the guarantee of immortality: how can we ensure the memory of those who have no name or heritage, no parents, wives, or friends? "Once they walked in the fields / And once again it is proper that they be remembered." "He walked in the fields," an image of the sabra, is transferred here by the poet to another essence, that of Holocaust survivors. Sivan does not point an accusing finger at anyone, but he underscores the past lives of the survivor recruits: the fact that they survived the death camps, only to die an anonymous death in the fields of Latrun. "What can one inscribe on the monument of such a recruit, / a man nameless and without family? The number / of the SS etched in his flesh?" The experience of the Holocaust, which in Alterman's poem is present but veiled, is starkly exposed here. Alterman described the battle of the Seventh Brigade within the context of a great campaign. Sivan's battle for Latrun takes place in a closed world, devoid of historical context. Whereas in Alterman the death of the immigrants is vindicated by opening the route to Jerusalem, Sivan does not give his readers the satisfaction of recompense. The poem is meant to secure the immortality of the unknown and nameless and their place in memory.

The most famous and provocative of the poems dealing with Latrun is that by Gabi Daniel (pseudonym of Binyamin Harushovsky), "Peter ha-gadol" (Peter the Great):

Peter the Great paved Petersburg
in the swamps of the north
on the bones of peasants.
David Ben-Gurion
paved
the way to the Burma Road,
the route to the road leading to the capital Jerusalem,
on the bones of boys from the Holocaust.
58

This poem contains a reversal of the myth of the Ingathering of the Exiles, undermining the dichotomy of "Holocaust and rebirth" (
shoah u-tekumah
). The survivors are presented as passive, their voices are not heard, they have no desire of their own. The others, the Israelis, instrumentalize them as objects. The poet appropriates the memory of the battle for Latrun and mythologizes it. The entire sacrifice is presented as that of the new immigrants. There is no trace here of the elements of human error, weakness, "no choice," or tragedy. What remains is the arrogant arbitrariness that strips the individual of his freedom of choice and humanity, turning him into a tiny cog in the grand machinery of historical events.

"Whenever memory is invoked we should be asking ourselves: by whom, where, in which context, against what?"
59
 That statement also applies to the case under consideration. What is Harushovsky's memory of the War of Independence? What does he long for, what reality does he find lacking? The research literature on historical memory has already noted that "memory is, of course, a substitute, surrogate or consolation for something that is missing."
60
 In his poem cycle, Harushovsky counterposes the collective identity of the survivors to the collective identity of the 
yishuv
, a new assessment of the relations between the absorbing   
yishuv
 and the absorbed immigrants. What was internalized as self-evident by Harushovsky, the young immigrant who carved out a place for himself in Israel, searching for a mooring so as to identify with Israeli culture and society, is rejected by the adult poet, estranged from the Israeli identity of the 1980s. Hayyim Guri, who published a harsh critique of the poem, touched on the question of memory. "I did not imagine that he, Daniel/Binyamin, would use this thing in 
such a way
, that this would be the meaning he gives today to those years."
61
 The focus of Harushovsky's identification ceased to be Israeli reality and returned to earlier vistas of his childhood memories and a cultural identity that had been suppressed, a sense of resentment and alienation that had been hidden under the surface of consciousness. To a certain degree, he became the voice for other survivors--those who after long years of silence had unburdened their heavy sense of alienation and the mute pain of the years of absorption and assimilation. Yet for most of those immigrants, voicing their accusations tended to strengthen their links with Israeli identity. Venting their anger helped reshape that identity in a new form. In Harushovsky's case, it was a moral justification to break the links to Israeli identity.

The emotions sparked by this poem and the public debate to which it gave rise underscored once more the nexus between literature and collective memory. This poem could not have been written a decade earlier: a change had been necessary in the spirit of the times for such lines to be written. The memory of the Holocaust and the sense of guilt toward the survivors had been raised to the top of the public agenda, exemplified by Aharon Appelfeld's 
Mikhvat ha-or
 (Scars of Light; 1982). The culture of the Palmah generation had lost its attraction for the Israeli public, and the war in Lebanon had cast doubts on the basic values of Israeli society. Israeli identity had been refashioned.
62

The undermining of Israeli identity was even more pronounced in the case of Matti Meged, who was chief editor of the "Palmah leaflet," one of the editors of the 
Sefer ha-Palmah
, and a member of the 
yishuv
 elite. He set out to deconstruct the memory of those days, thus articulating a protest against contemporary Israeli realities. He used the events at Latrun as a point of encounter between the living and the dead, assimilators and the assimilated, morality and history, past and present, memory and reality.

Meged recounted his version of Latrun for the first time after the Six-Day War, when Collins and Lapierre interviewed him while working on their book 
O, Jerusalem
. He told the interviewer how, as a staff officer of the Haganah in Europe, he had accompanied immigrants on the ship 
Kalanit
 to Israel's shores, arriving with them in Haifa right after the proclamation of the state on May 15, 1948. At the port, a black Oldsmobile sedan was waiting and took him directly to a meeting with Ben-Gurion. The "old man" expressed interest in the immigrants and asked about their military training. He then informed the astonished Meged that the immigrants were to be sent immediately into battle. According to Meged, he protested this decision, but Ben-Gurion responded by saying there was no choice. Within 72 hours of the immigrants' arrival, Meged continued, they had been dispatched to the front at Latrun. Meged was with them. Under heavy fire at Latrun, the men were like frightened animals. They did not know how to use their weapons; the safety latches were locked. A young immigrant, gasping his last breath, whispered in Meged's ear: "We've let you down."
63
 Meged's story was later retold in a shorter version contained in Michael Bar-Zohar's 
Ben-Gurion
.
64

No one raised doubts about the authenticity of the story or the messages it contained, since it differed little from the accounts and rumors that had circulated in the Palmah tents after the Latrun battle. Moreover, the tale about the controversy with Ben-Gurion, the lack of experience among the immigrants under fire, the meeting on the battlefield between the veteran member of the  
yishuv
 and the dying new immigrant, and his final words were all part of a body of literary narrative patterns that were familiar in the discursive context of Latrun. As mentioned, Yigal Mosinsohn had made use of these topoi in his popular play "Be-arvot ha-Negev," transforming them in the process into part of the collective memory of Latrun. The accusation of hard-heartedness that Meged hurls at Ben-Gurion was accepted as the conventional view among both Ben-Gurion's admirers and his opponents. What his antagonists regarded as a lack of humanity, his supporters pointed to as proof of his strength of leadership in a time of crisis. Meged's story was thus absorbed into the corpus of narratives on the War of Independence more generally and the body of tales spun around Latrun specifically.

The storm began when Meged repeated his story in 1987, during a visit to Israel from his home-in-exile, New York. Interviewed by Tamar Mhroz in 
Haaretz
 (January 9), Meged did not use Latrun merely as a way to attack and criticize Ben-Gurion within the legitimate and accepted framework of the "other version." Rather, he now treated Latrun as a symbol of (and proof for) the need for radical revision: nothing in the early days of the state had occurred in the way it had been presented and constructed; everything had to be reexamined. Latrun became part of Meged's journey to the past, a trek heavy with bitterness, disappointment, irony, and disillusionment. "In that journey backward in time to scenes of the past, it is not clear whether it's all real or just imaginary. Things alter their appearance. Nothing is as it was." This description, where Meged sketches the nature of his new book, also reflects his own psychological mood as he embarks on an assessment of his personal past. "How as a Palmahnik did I 
really
 bring illegal immigrants to Palestine?" What in the past had been bold and heroic now became a sham: "The whole thing was so foolish"; "It was all so clumsy." The message of the present to the past is evident in almost every line: "There was something grotesque there right from the beginning, but in all honesty, it took me quite a good many years to comprehend that." The meeting with the survivors is described as an encounter between the sabras--arrogant and unfeeling, whose attitude toward the survivors is patronizing and full of contempt--and new immigrants, who have only affection and admiration for the native sons. "Only many years later did I start to feel the burning ache of shame and guilt." Meged is conscious of the sea change that has taken place in his memory: "Sometimes I wonder whether I'm the only one who, from a distance, sees things today in a different light, sober, cruel"; "My past is evaporating, and nothing remains of it."

In Meged's case, Latrun plays a key role in the process of the vaporization of the past. It is evidence of the distance between proud words and actual deeds: the heroic tales replete with brave exploits on the "escape" (
berihah
) from Europe and "illegal immigration" (
haapalah
) on the one hand, and the bungling, blundering actuality on the other; the rhetoric of "bearing the people on their shoulders" versus the reality of immigrants plodding through heavy snow in northern Italy; the pretension of giving the immigrants military training versus the reality of a few measly drills; the praise for equality heard from Palmah members sent as trainers to the displaced-persons camps in Germany versus the fact that they themselves chose to live outside those camps; and finally, the heroic story of the 
Kalanit
