 arriving on the shores of Palestine versus the reality of its human cargo, harried and weakened by sea sickness. Meged went on at greater length to describe his meeting with Ben-Gurion, his protest against Ben-Gurion's intention to send the immigrants into combat, his complaint to Yigal Allon, the Palmah commander, and his joining of his disciples who went off to battle. Meged said that he had heard Shlomoh Shamir proclaim: "We're no longer an underground! We don't have to operate now at night! We'll go in broad daylight!" This was followed by the description of the battle at Latrun and the final moving words of the dying immigrant: "We've let you down."

There is enormous power in the claim of an eyewitness: "I was there." Whereas Harushovsky put a distance between himself and the autobiographical components of his poem (by means of the pseudonym Gabi Daniel), Meged bore upon himself the experiences of others, internalizing them as if they were his own. What in 1972 had been a kind of collective tall tale, documenting the standard version of events at Latrun, now became a pointed indictment. It was an accusation directed against the whole system of relations between Israel and the Diaspora, the redeemers and the redeemed, the arrogance of the army command and the purity of sacrifice by the immigrant recruits. The target of the assault here was the entire edifice of the Israeli establishment, and no distinction was made between the Palmah and Ben-Gurion.

The fanciful element in the story was that Meged, so far as is known, had not been a member of the Haganah general staff in Europe and did not come to Israel in May 1948. The ship 
Kalanit
 did not dock in Haifa until July 1948. The immigrants who disembarked from it did take part in combat in the War of Independence, but not in Latrun. The story of his meeting with Ben-Gurion and the conversation that ensued, the meeting with Allon, the quote from Shamir, the description of combat at Latrun, and the last words of the immigrant there--all of these elements were fictional. Hayyim Guri, in a letter to 
Haaretz
 (January 16, 1987), stated outright that Meged was not a "member of the staff of the Haganah in Europe," as he had (mis)represented himself; he did not bring a ship of illegal immigrants in May 1948 but arrived from France on the 
Kalanit
 on July 4. Patently, his entire story was pure fabrication. Shamir also declared that "Meged was not in Latrun at the time of the battle, and obviously did not hear those lies from me. The other details he added are all fictional and bereft of truth" (
Haaretz
, February 3, 1987).

Reactions from the public to Meged's interview were polarized: one letter to 
Haaretz
 complained that the editorial board had not checked the truth of the facts before publishing the article. Had it done so, it would have spared its readers "depressing conclusions based on fraudulent facts, apparently derived from Meged's profound personal frustration." Another letter claimed that the article reflected the disillusionment felt by "this people" in the wake of the Yom Kipur War. "I have never encountered such a profound critique of all the basic concepts which we were raised on and which we ourselves cultivated." The writer ends with praise for Meged and adds: "It is good to see things in the proper light and not to hide behind foggy memories of a past that was distant and good."
65
 In a series of responses and counter-replies between Meged, the poet Natan Zakh, and Hayyim Guri, facts were intermixed with fiction, memory with history, the past with the present. Guri attempted to distinguish between the "rottenness" of the present and the memory of the past, between criticism based on reality and that rooted in fiction and invention. Meged and Zakh refused to recognize the absoluteness of that distinction. Does the past shape the present, or is it the other way round? Are facts something that occur empirically, that can be documented and mapped, or are they merely in someone's head? Is an individual's recollection of events less valid than the picture drawn by documents and testimony? Meged admitted that in the 
Haaretz
 interview he made reference to a novel he was working on, and he "was not careful enough in drawing the line between the 'hero' of the novel and myself." However, to his mind, that does not invalidate the internal truth expressed in the interview: namely the attempt to locate the roots of the contemporary malaise afflicting Israel. The rhetoric of the past planted fraudulent norms in Israeli society--a reluctance to face the truth and the cultivation of corruption and self-glorification. Distinguishing between his personal (fictitious) story and the events at Latrun, he protested: "Isn't it the truth that untrained immigrants who only just arrived were rushed into battle, and that many of them also died there?" To the present day, he contended, the slogan 
ein brerah
 (no choice) continues to cloak and whitewash "all the superfluous failures and callous indifference to unnecessary victims, and even crimes." As to whether he was actually in Latrun, Meged asserted: "I was not meticulous with regard to details, and I don't remember many of them precisely any more. 
But I was there and experienced what I told about. No documents from archives or other evidence can disprove that truth.
 Yet that's really not what's important."
66

Meged questioned the established version of history as interpreted by the tools of the discipline. To this he counterposed the personal internalization of historical events, similar to a documentary drama that mixes fact and fiction yet presents the 
internal truth
 of the events as understood by the author. The pattern of events as fashioned in the imagination of the individual is a recollection of the events as they were 
supposed
 to have happened. "These past thirty-five years, I've been carrying around that story inside me, as if I'd really been there" (as Guri quoted a remark made by Meged).
67

The circle opened up by Harushovsky's poems and Meged's complaints was closed by Natan Zakh. Zakh contended that Meged's claims proved the veracity of Harushovsky's poems: the State of Israel was born in the sin of hypocrisy and pretence, and upon the blood of the Holocaust survivors. The tale told by Harushovsky from the perspective of the illegal immigrants was now recounted by Meged from the standpoint of those absorbing the immigrants. The truth in Meged's story, Zakh argued, was more important that the factual details, "and all the rest is written in the history books, with footnotes and quotes, and all the examined facts: just how many, from what countries, how many sabras and how many 'Gahal' men, etc., etc." Even if Meged was not precise in what he said, Zakh wrote, "the truth in his assertions is evident. And if this is the case with true words, how much more so when it comes to 
true feelings
."
68

Meged's disenchantment with Israeli identity was bound up with his breaking free from memories of the past. Memory had become a burden, obstructing his psychological rehabilitation, his building of a new identity. Just as the creation of a common identity requires inventing a common past, the dismantling of that same identity demands jettisoning a shared memory. In the Israel of the 1980s, such an attempt at dismantling identity met with mixed feelings. Although criticism of the foundation myth of the state was accepted and even fashionable at the time, the majority of the public was not prepared to go quite that far. By the early 1990s, the version of Latrun used to deconstruct the myth of the Ingathering of the Exiles remained confined to a small group within the critical intelligentsia, whose scathing critique of Israeli society was broad, incisive, and unambiguously political.
69

Conclusion

Latrun exemplifes the mythopoeic dynamic: how a myth crystallizes around a certain kernel of fact and then constructs and molds collective memory. The ideology behind the myth changes with time. The social groups that are aided and empowered by the myth also alter and shift. Yet the symbol that has been created does not lose its centrality and salience. Pierre Nora observed that memory links up with spatial sites, whereas history is riveted to events. I am not convinced of the accuracy of this distinction between the spatial and the chronological. Yet there is no doubt that collective memory seizes upon symbols like that of Latrun. Against the accepted narrative, a counter-version appears that represents those who feel slighted by the standard reading, which has not given them their due place in historical annals. That counter-version is based principally on personal testimony and memory rather than on official documentation. Its strength does not lie in its factual veracity but in its ability to seize the imagination. It does not represent history as it was but rather as it should have been--if the proper expression had been given to social groups and diverse cultural currents. Shared memory is a foundation for common identity. In the battle for national identity, "identity-defining functions of memory"
70
 acquire enormous significance. Thus, whereas academic historiography attempts to determine how and why things occurred, the first task of collective memory is to forge a common national bond. In the case of Latrun, a changing Israeli subidentity found its symbolic mooring, shaping the myth. In commenting on the deconstructive fashion of "smashing the myths" of the War of Independence, S. Yizhar characterized the relation between present and past: "All maturation is an examination of the beginnings. And any examination is both in order to learn and in order to break free from the past and to justify that separation."
71

An analysis of the Latrun case highlights the limitations of historiography in molding collective memory. It appears justified to formulate a kind of "iron law of the devaluation of the past": the worse the news about the past, the stronger the tendency to believe it. The readiness to accept any and all bad news about the past and to internalize it, and to disregard "good news" about the past as not authentic or credible, is a collective phenomenon that encompasses the educated and unschooled alike, old-time members of the 
yishuv
 and new immigrants, and even people of the establishment and of the counter-establishment. This readiness is well exemplified by the growing gap between what actually occurred at Latrun and the public image of the battle, despite repeated attempts from various sources to present the public with the unadorned historical facts. To explicate this phenomenon is a complex task; its roots should be sought in the specific sociocultural and social-psychological features of Israeli society.

Part of the explanation can be found in the ways Israeli society relates to its past. Wherever romantic proclivities are a powerful social force, a tendency can develop to idealize and embellish the past, especially more distant decades. That past serves as an essential opposite pole, the "Golden Age" counterposed to the gray and corrupt reality of the present. However, in a society whose members share a strong spirit of revolt, there is a tendency to paint the past, particularly the more recent past, in black colors and exaggerate its grotesque features. Such a phenomenon is a pronounced feature in how revolutionary societies relate to the traditional or bourgeois societies that they aspire to supplant.

Characteristic of our post-modern society is a pervasive loss of innocence, the bankruptcy of the grand faiths and ideologies. To suffice pragmatically with a non-ideal world is an integral part of modern existence and ethos. Any attempt to represent the past, both distant or more recent, in idealizing hues is thus perceived as phoney and meets with a dubious smile. By contrast, to make heavy use of dark tones in depicting past events is regarded as authentic, since it meshes with a more general social tendency in relating to political, social, or intellectual reality. A downbeat approach to the present and skepticism about the future are extended and projected onto the past--in some ways perhaps a new variant of the Marxian principle that reality molds consciousness, including consciousness of the past.

In earlier eras, the ruling elites tended to monopolize memory. Today memory has changed from an instrument for glorifying the dominant elites into a means undermining their credibility and helping to multiply the foci of authority in society. No longer are there isolated and limited centers of inspiration and legitimacy that enjoy prestige and credibility. Now authority gravitates to unexpected and esoteric foci, whose power flows from their location at critical junctions that open up access to the general social psyche. The print and electronic media provide their agents with a position seemingly external to the establishment--one that pretends to represent independent opinion, unbiased and uncorrupted, and is thus more "truthful" than views attributed to the political elites or the academy. The response of the media to the public's dubiousness and penchant for pessimism abets the "iron law of the devaluation of the past."

The predilection today to be naturally suspicious of authoritative truths is the very basis of the process of transmission and reception of a depreciated image of the past's value. Criticism of the present alienates people from those basic myths that underpin the existing order and endow it with intrinsic value. Just as myths act by appealing to the imagination, to sentiments, and to a transcendental image of reality, their demolition uses those same instrumentalities. In this context, literary elites have an important role to play. Literature is able to penetrate the protective sheath of logic that society has woven for its self-preservation. Via sentiments and irrational imaginings of reality, literature projects its messages into the depths of consciousness. It conveys a mode of authenticity that is not amenable to analytical dissection using the customary categories of "truth" or "falsehood." Thus, even if it has no pretensions about claiming to "describe" reality, literature is able to transmit messages that are 
prima facie
 historical and that most certainly shape memory, beaming them deep into the national psyche. Thus, even if only a relatively small group of intellectual elites are receptive to ideas that serve to shatter the myth of the Ingathering of the Exiles, the historical narrative circling around it and attempting to demolish it, namely the story of Latrun, is given a powerful impetus. In sharp contrast to ideological elements, the literary narrative can affect broad segments of the population. Compared with the penetrating power of that message, the voice of the historian is of but feeble significance.

In its variant as the myth of the new immigrants and their part and sacrifice in the War of Independence, Latrun continues to gather potency: anyone wishing to participate in that myth will relate himself in some way to the battle that raged there. Just as the number of immigrants who claimed they came to Palestine on the 
Altalena
 (the ship of the Irgun) would, if true, have been enough to send the vessel to the bottom of the Mediterranean, the number of those who maintain they walked in the (battle)fields at Latrun continues to mount.

In 1993, the official organ of the Israeli Air Force published an adventurous account about a group of 40 immigrants from India who flew to Israel via Cyprus. As the story goes, they arrived from Cyprus on the very eve of the establishment of the state. And, of course, they were sent to Latrun. According to the author, 28 of them lost their lives on that battlefield, and another 8 were wounded. Just as in legends, where one is not supposed (or be able) to check the hard facts, the article notes that the lists with the names of those Indian immigrants were also destroyed in the battle.
72

The myth of Latrun lives on.

 To my mind, the most sensitive matter in this connection is the question of the conscription of only children. A short time after the beginning of hostilities, in February 1948, when the terrible tragedy suffered by families who had lost their only child became evident, an order was issued to exempt men who were the sole child in their family from combat duty. Soon thereafter, an "only child" was defined as the "sole child of parents living in the Land of Israel and without sisters" (Yablonka, 
Ahim zarim
, 139-43. She cites the protocol of the Executive Committee, Central Command of National Service, March 28, 1948, IDF Archives, 679/56/21). This order excluded the sole sons of families who experienced the Holocaust, who were often the only remaining members of those families. Sivan notes that among the immigrants who entered Palestine in 1946 and 1947 and died in battle, at least 30 percent were orphans or had no relatives in Palestine (Sivan, 
Dor Tashah

According to Yablonka, the directive was worked out because there were fears that a more liberal one would lead to a situation where a large segment of those obliged to serve would be exempted. Yablonka also refers to the lack of understanding and internalization of the nature of the Shoah within the 
yishuv
 and its leadership at that juncture. The survivors seldom raised the issue at that time. But after many years, the sense of bitterness over this discrimination mounted once again. In testimony given to me by Abba Kovner regarding his meeting with the leadership of the 
yishuv

Kovner told about the attitude of a Soviet-Jewish commander, one of the liberators of Vilna, who refused to accept him and other Jewish partisans into his units, saying "you already did your share." Kovner turned my attention to the question of only children and spoke with deep bitterness about the fact that only children in the

 In this connection, it is useful to recall the story of Mosheh Zanbar. The narrative's transformations and perambulations can shed light both on the question of new immigrants and the way in which Latrun became a focus for identity. Zanbar arrived on May 30, 1948, from Marseille on a boat carrying immigrants. He was conscripted and inducted at the recruit center, and sent with a group of some 100 new immigrants to work as a porter on the Burma Road (June 7-8). A convoy of jeeps from Jerusalem approached the porters. One of the jeeps turned over and fell on Zanbar's leg, injuring him badly. He had terrible pain from the open fracture, so much that the rough motion of the Jeep made it impossible to evacuate him in that vehicle. He was left alone in the dark until 2 or 3 a.m., when another patrol arrived and took Zanbar to the hospital.

This story is part of the chapter on the opening of the Burma Road. It also reflects the sense of alienation felt by a new immi-grant abandoned in the field at a difficult moment in his life. However, it has no connection with the battle for Latrun or Operation Bin-Nun A. In this regard, Yitshaki (226) showed a lack of circumspection: he wrote that Zanbar was injured in the Battle Bin-Nun A, as a soldier of the 72nd Battalion, and that he crawled for two days, badly wounded, dragging himself over the ground in order to reach IDF forces. The substantiation he presented for this is the book by Yuval Elitsur and Eliyahu Salpeter, 
Ha-mimsad
 (Tel Aviv, 1973), 157. An examination of this source indicates that it indeed states that Zanbar was injured at the "Latrun front" and was thought dead, but nothing is said about his crawling for two days, nor is it clear in which of the Latrun battles he was wounded. In the 1989 television program "Shever anan," Zanbar was exact in describing when he arrived in the Latrun theater of operations, his job as a porter and the circumstances of his injury. However, since the director of the program made a link between him and one of the fighters at Latrun, TV viewers were given the false impression that his wounding and abandonment were part of the story of Battle Bin-Nun A. My thanks to Shlomoh Shamir, who suggested I examine the testimony of Zanbar, January 1, 1986, which was presented to him that year and on which I have based my comments.
